correctness.rationale: For either unextended family, two nonzero dual weights imply external distance two, hence Delsarte gives covering radius at most two. Minimum distance three and \(N=n+1<2^r\) exclude radius one by the perfect-code sphere identity, so the punctured radius is exactly two. In the parity extension, the last syndrome bit is error parity. Every nonzero last-zero syndrome therefore has leader weight exactly two; among last-one syndromes the \(N\) distinct parity-check columns have weight one, and every remaining syndrome is represented by two base columns plus the new parity column, hence has leader weight three. Thus \(L_0=1,L_1=N,L_2=2^r-1,L_3=2^r-N\) and the radius is three. Fresh independent arithmetic reproduced \((1,52,255,204)\) for Family A at \(s=2\) and \((1,86,255,170)\) for Family B at \(s=4\).
residual_risks: The theorem covers only the two distance-four parity-extension families whose punctured duals have exactly two nonzero weights.

originality.rationale: Chen-Xie-Ding explicitly leave the covering radii of their distance-optimal families as Open Problem 8.6. Their Theorems 4.2/6.2 provide the two-weight dual data for the punctured codes and Theorems 4.5/6.5 provide the distance-four extensions, but they do not state the extension radii or coset-leader distributions. Delsarte alone determines only the punctured radius; the parity-syndrome lifting lemma is the additional step that fixes every extended coset. Targeted searches found no earlier theorem or table containing these two exact extended-family results.
residual_risks: An older general parity-extension lemma may make the syndrome lifting step classical even if these exact family consequences were not located.
